rv.q: The actress’s stage debut in Anna Ziegler’s Evening All Afternoon makes for an affecting portrait of grief Dominic Cavendish has been writing about theatre and comedy since the mid-1990s and became the Telegraph's lead theatre critic in 2014. See more He is the founding editor of the leading audio resource theatrevoice.com, now run by the V&A.
The young actor is burningly charismatic – and probably would be in most roles – but it’s the combination of insouciant swagger and cataclysmic fragility that draws us to her.

Anna Ziegler’s world premiere play runs until 11 April It begins hesitantly, with an awkward joke about joining a step class as a stepmother and stepdaughter. But as Anna Ziegler’s play unfolds, it becomes something else – a surprising and quietly powerful study of grief and families.

The pair are thrown together when Jennifer marries Delilah’s father, John, in writer Anna Ziegler’s new play. Following the sudden death of her loving mother, Delilah (Erin Kellyman) is an angry, attitudinising teenager. Also coming to terms with the loss of her mother, Jennifer (Anastasia Hille) is a mouse of a woman.
In its restraint lies its impact: a finely made play, delivered with a level of care and craft that makes its modest scale feel genuinely rewarding.
Ultimately, Afternoon is a reflective, compassionate exploration of a modern family life and a difficult relationship, imperfect in places but aware that understanding must be spoken into being.
It all looks stylish but isn't easy to interpret
Ultimately, the script is too comfortable to have any impact.
Afternoon tries to do too many things at the same time, drawing in lightly explored mental health challenges.
